title: AI is Problematic. Why Does PAIRR Use it?
author: Julie Gamberg, Marit MacArthur, Anna Mills, Aparna Sinha, and Lisa Sperber
summary: Written by the writing instructors behind the PAIRR (Peer and AI Review plus Reflection) project, this statement addresses students directly and explains why a program that acknowledges serious ethical problems with AI still invites them to use AI feedback on their writing. The authors lay out the major concerns in turn: environmental costs from data center growth, uncertainty about job loss and the exploitation of data workers, bias built into training data, and intellectual property questions. For each, they pair an honest account of the harm with individual choices students can make and a case for collective, democratic oversight. The essay's central move is to argue that consumer choices alone cannot ensure responsible AI, and that writing teachers, not technology companies, should guide how students use these tools. It presents PAIRR as a way to build AI literacy and skeptical habits of questioning AI output alongside human peer review, and invites students to comment on the statement before deciding whether to opt in.
points: The authors frame PAIRR as teaching students to question AI feedback alongside peer feedback rather than simply adopting it.
They note that smaller, purpose-built models, not large generative systems, drive most successful power grid optimization, citing Jon Ippolito.
Individual choices such as avoiding AI for trivial tasks and choosing efficient models are encouraged, but regulation is described as essential.
The statement argues that bias cannot be trained out of models because they reproduce patterns in web-scale training data dominated by wealthy, well-represented groups.
Students are invited to comment on the statement before choosing whether to opt in to the program.
quotes: For the PAIRR project, we believe AI feedback can potentially help students revise their writing, because AI has access to strategies drawn from writing teachers. However, like many of you reading this, we have serious concerns about AI.
Crucially, as Jon Ippolito points out, we don’t need large generative AI models–or new data centers–to improve power efficiency.
But consumer choices are not enough. Just as markets and consumer choices alone can’t ensure clean air, water, safe food, or drugs, they won’t ensure sustainable AI.
We argue that the uncertainty about AI’s impacts on jobs, and serious labor concerns, point to the need for informed democratic oversight of AI.
We strongly believe that writing teachers should guide how students use AI, so they can learn how to use AI responsibly and ethically.
Since AI reflects patterns from its “data,” it will continue to default toward stereotypical perspectives.

A single image like this might not seem like a big deal. But when these patterns repeat across countless AI-generated images and texts, they reinforce, amplify and even normalize ethnic, gender, class and other forms of bias and stereotypes.
